Friedrich Hayek, who lived from eighteen ninety-nine to nineteen ninety-two, was an Austrian-born economist and political philosopher who championed free markets, individual liberty, and decentralized knowledge as arguments against central planning and socialism. Winner of the Nobel Prize in Economics in nineteen seventy-four, he profoundly influenced modern conservatism and libertarianism, though his ideas were often caricatured and contested. He argued that centrally planned economies cannot succeed because no authority can gather and process the dispersed knowledge held by millions of individuals. Markets solve this problem through price signals. In his book The Road to Serfdom, published in nineteen forty-four, he contended that even well-intentioned central planning, by concentrating power, tends toward totalitarianism, and that individual liberty and the rule of law are prerequisites for prosperity. He defended laissez-faire capitalism not as perfect but as the system most compatible with human liberty and knowledge generation. He critiqued John Maynard Keynes and interventionist macroeconomics, arguing that artificial stimulus distorts prices and leads to unsustainable booms and busts. He influenced Milton Friedman and the Chicago School, both of whom defended market economics against the Keynesian consensus that dominated mid-twentieth-century thought. He believed that spontaneous order—complex social structures arising without central design—is the source of innovation and efficiency, not just in markets but in law and culture. He saw Karl Marx's central planning as impossible and tyrannical, standing at the opposite pole of economic thought. His defense of markets and critique of Keynesian interventionism were shared by Milton Friedman. His intellectual rivalry with John Maynard Keynes, whose theory of demand and interventionist approach he opposed, shaped twentieth-century economics. In the domain of international trade, Hayek championed free trade against protectionism.
